title: Backlog-driven quality planning, control and acceptance
blurb: Explain what drives the quality practice in PRINCE2 Agile, and how quality is planned, controlled and accepted iteration by iteration.
question: A board member asks how quality will be managed on an agile project when there is no big test phase at the end. What drives the quality practice, and what cycle does it follow?

teach.body: The quality practice exists to document the users' requirements of the project products and to set up the means by which those requirements will be met. Put simply, it answers: what is acceptable to the users, and how will we measure it? Quality here means the characteristics that make the project products fit for purpose and in line with expectations.

In PRINCE2 Agile the quality practice is driven by the requirements held in the project backlog. A repeating cycle of quality planning, quality control and product acceptance keeps the project products aligned with the project's quality management approach. Because the backlog is refined all the time, quality is planned in small pieces, close to when the work happens, not all at once at the start.

teach.caption: The project backlog replaces the project product description; the product backlog replaces product descriptions (8.3.2.1).

steps.label: Iteration
steps.sub: test or check as you go

teach.body: Quality control runs inside the iteration: testers design and run tests or quality reviews and check products against acceptance criteria and the team DoD. When executing a work package, the team tells the project manager about completed quality activities and products and obtains approvals. Acceptance is frequent: completed features are shown in the product demo topic of the progress review workshop, and the closure workshop has a final product demo.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table 13.10, Table 13.12, Table 13.19

teach.body: Tamarside Buses is replacing paper tickets with a mobile app. Chief product owner Grace Adeyemi keeps the project backlog, where the epic 'buy a day ticket' links to the project DoD. Product owner Tomasz Nowak's team refines stories each iteration, adding testable acceptance criteria. Tester Priya Raman checks each story as it is built, and at the progress review drivers try the ticket screen in the product demo and give acceptance and feedback.

teach.text: The quality practice is driven by the requirements in the PROJECT BACKLOG, through quality planning, quality control and product acceptance. It is not driven by the Agilometer (a risk tool), and acceptance is not saved for one event at the end of the project.

teach.body: If the business already has its own product design, development and testing procedures, they may be used instead of the standard one. That choice is recorded as a tailoring decision in the PID. Quality can also flex: under the focus on products principle, product descriptions, quality specifications and quality tolerances can be prioritized and broken down so that what is delivered can vary.

Driven by the project backlog; cycle of quality planning, quality control, product acceptance (9.3.1).

summary: You can now explain that the quality practice in PRINCE2 Agile is driven by the project backlog through a cycle of quality planning, quality control and product acceptance. You can also say where quality criteria live and how acceptance happens frequently rather than at the end.

A.q: What is the purpose of the quality practice?
options: Control changes to the project's baseline
Monitor actual achievements against those planned
Document users' requirements and how they will be met
Identify and control uncertainties affecting objectives
A.why: The quality practice documents the users' requirements of the project products and establishes the means by which they will be met (9.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling changes to the baseline is the purpose of the issues practice.
whyNot.1: Comparing actual achievements with the plan is the progress practice.
whyNot.3: Controlling uncertainties that affect objectives is the risk practice.

A.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what drives the quality practice?
options: The requirements held in the project backlog
The Agilometer assessment of the project
The risks recorded in the risk register
The tolerances set in the project canvas
A.why: The quality practice is driven by the requirements expressed in the project backlog (9.3.1).

whyNot.1: The Agilometer is a risk practice tool for the risks of agile working, not the driver of quality.
whyNot.2: The risk register records risks; it does not drive quality planning.
whyNot.3: The project canvas gives business justification; it does not drive the quality cycle.

A.q: Which question does the quality practice help answer?
options: Why does the project exist and what must it stay aligned to?
What now, when a product deviates from what was agreed?
What if something unexpected happens, and how do we respond?
What is acceptable to the users and how can it be measured?
A.why: Table 5.2 links the quality practice to the question of what is acceptable to the users and how this can be measured.

whyNot.0: Why the project exists and what it stays aligned to is the business case question.
whyNot.1: Responding when a product deviates from what was agreed is the issues question.
whyNot.2: Responding to the unexpected is the risk practice question.

B.q: Which cycle aligns the project products with the quality management approach in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Identify, assess, plan, implement, communicate
Quality planning, quality control, product acceptance
Develop, check, maintain, confirm the business case
Capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement
B.why: Driven by the project backlog, the quality practice runs a cycle of quality planning, quality control and product acceptance (9.3.1).

whyNot.0: Identify, assess, plan, implement, communicate are the risk management steps.
whyNot.2: Develop, check, maintain, confirm describe the business case cycle.
whyNot.3: Capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement describe handling issues.

B.q: A supplier wants to use its own well-proven design, development and testing procedure instead of the standard one. How should this be handled?
options: Raise it as an issue for the change authority to decide
Record it in the quality register as a planned activity
Record it as a tailoring decision in the PID
Add it to the product backlog as a new user story
B.why: An organization's own procedure may be used, and that choice is documented as a tailoring decision in the PID (9.3.1).

whyNot.0: Choosing a procedure is a tailoring decision made in initiation, not a request for change.
whyNot.1: The quality register records quality activities and results, not tailoring decisions.
whyNot.3: A procedure is not a product requirement, so it does not belong in the product backlog.

B.q:
Which two statements about quality in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Acceptance criteria are kept with user stories in the product backlog.
2. User acceptance is gathered once, in the final product demo.
3. Quality control takes place inside each iteration.
4. Quality criteria are fixed in full before the first iteration.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
B.why: Stories in the product backlog carry their acceptance criteria (1), and quality control happens as the work is built in each iteration (3) (9.3.1, 9.4.3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: users give acceptance and feedback in product demos throughout, not once.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: acceptance is frequent, and quality criteria are refined along with the backlog.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: criteria are refined with the backlog rather than fixed in full up front.

C.q: Which artifact holds the epics and shows the project Definition of Done, and which role owns it?
options: Product backlog; product owner
Quality register; project support
Team dashboard; team coach
Project backlog; chief product owner
C.why: The project backlog holds high-level epics, shows or links the project DoR and DoD and names who accepts the project product; the CPO owns it (8.3.2.1, Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: The product backlog holds a team's user stories and links the team DoD, not the project DoD.
whyNot.1: The quality register records quality activities and results; it does not hold epics.
whyNot.2: The team dashboard reports team progress and is not owned by the team coach.

C.q: In which workshop topic do users see completed features and give acceptance and feedback during a stage?
options: Product demo in the progress review workshop
Iteration planning in the team planning workshop
Project highlights in the project kickoff workshop
Release planning in the release planning workshop
C.why: The product demo topic of the progress review workshop shows completed features and gathers user acceptance and feedback (Table 13.10).

whyNot.1: Iteration planning selects stories for the next iteration and produces the team plan.
whyNot.2: The kickoff workshop builds the team and its dashboards; it does not demo finished features.
whyNot.3: Release planning updates the release map and OKRs at a stage boundary.

C.q: During 'execute a work package', what does the team do about quality?
options: Approves the quality management approach on behalf of the board
Notifies the PM of completed quality activities and gets approvals
Agrees the project tolerances for quality with the executive
Replaces the acceptance criteria with the team's own DoR
C.why: When executing a work package the team notifies the project manager of completed quality activities and products and obtains approvals for completed products (Table 13.12).

whyNot.0: The quality management approach is agreed in initiating a project and approved by the board.
whyNot.2: Project tolerances are set by the board, not by the team in managing product delivery.
whyNot.3: The DoR controls when work may start; it does not replace acceptance criteria.

reteach.title: A kitchen that tastes as it cooks
reteach.question: Why does an agile team check quality all the way through instead of at the end?

blocks.body: A good chef does not cook a whole banquet and taste it only when the guests sit down. Each dish has a recipe (the quality criteria), the chef tastes while cooking (quality control) and the head waiter checks each plate before it leaves (acceptance). The order book is the project backlog: it decides what gets cooked and what 'good' looks like.

blocks.text: Quality planning, quality control and product acceptance repeat every iteration, driven by the project backlog. Do not mix this cycle up with the risk steps or the issue steps.

explain.body: The quality practice documents what users require of the project products and sets up how those requirements will be met. In agile terms: what is acceptable to users, and how will it be measured?

head: Practice
Core question
rows: What is acceptable and how is it measured?

test.q: Which practice documents the users' requirements of the project products?
options: Plans
Quality
Business case
Progress
test.why: Documenting users' requirements of the project products and how they will be met is the purpose of the quality practice (9.1).

whyNot.0: Plans defines the products and the means to deliver them, with estimates of when and how much.
whyNot.2: The business case judges whether the project is desirable, viable and achievable.
whyNot.3: Progress compares actual achievements with plans and forecasts.

explain.body: The requirements in the project backlog drive the practice. A cycle of quality planning, quality control and product acceptance keeps products aligned with the quality management approach.

test.q: Identify the missing words in the following sentence. In PRINCE2 Agile, the quality practice is driven by the requirements in the [?].
options: risk register
release map
project backlog
team dashboard
test.why: The quality practice is driven by the requirements expressed in the project backlog (9.3.1).

whyNot.0: The risk register records risks, not product requirements.
whyNot.1: The release map plans releases and iterations; it is a plan, not the requirements source.
whyNot.3: The team dashboard shows team progress.

explain.body: Each user story carries testable acceptance criteria; the product backlog links the team DoD; the project backlog shows the project DoR and DoD. Quality is planned close to the work.

test.q: Where are a team's user stories and their acceptance criteria held?
options: Product backlog
Project backlog
Quality register
Project canvas
test.why: The product backlog holds the team's user stories with their acceptance criteria and includes or links the team DoD (8.3.2.1).

whyNot.1: The project backlog holds high-level epics at project level.
whyNot.2: The quality register records planned and completed quality activities.
whyNot.3: The project canvas is the one-page business justification.

explain.body: Late quality checks are a known problem of traditional projects. In PRINCE2 Agile, users see finished features in product demos at progress reviews and give acceptance and feedback, so problems surface early.

test.q: Which traditional problem does frequent user acceptance help to address?
options: Teams estimating in absolute hours
Boards receiving too few reports
Quality being assessed late
Benefits being measured too often
test.why: Traditional projects tend to assess quality late in the lifecycle and miss chances to fix problems early (Table 2.2); frequent acceptance tackles this.

whyNot.0: Estimating style is a planning matter, not what frequent acceptance fixes.
whyNot.1: Report volume is a progress concern, not the quality problem described.
whyNot.3: Measuring benefits often is not a problem that frequent acceptance addresses.
